analysis.one_liner: Guarantees people in managed care plans access to specialists, emergency care, clinical trials, appeals, and full disclosure of plan rules.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced by one senator with no cosponsors, sent to the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee, and never received any further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have written a set of enforceable rights for people enrolled in HMOs and other managed care health plans. Plans would have had to provide enough doctors, standing referrals to specialists, direct access to OB-GYNs, emergency care without prior approval, coverage for clinical trials, outside appeals of denied care, and detailed disclosure of what is covered and how doctors are paid. It applied these rules to employer plans, individual insurance, Medicare and Medicaid managed care, and the federal employees' program, and let states add stricter rules. It never advanced past its first reading in the Senate.
analysis.who_benefits: People enrolled in managed care group plans and individual health insurance, including Medicare and Medicaid beneficiaries in managed care and federal employees. The bill's patient rights would apply to them: enough primary care doctors and specialists in the network, standing referrals for specialty care, direct access to obstetrician-gynecologists, emergency care judged by a 'prudent layperson' standard without prior authorization, coverage of routine costs in approved clinical trials for serious illnesses, continuity of care if a provider contract ends, outside review panels for appeals of denied care, medical-record confidentiality, and a short annual prospectus disclosing denial rates, doctor ratios, how physicians are paid, and how to appeal.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Managed care and health plan enrollees

how_it_helps.text: Requires plans to provide emergency services without prior authorization and defines an emergency from the perspective of a prudent layperson, so patients would not be billed for ER visits a plan later judged unnecessary.
Guarantees standing referrals to specialists, access to non-network providers, and direct access to OB-GYNs without a referral, including allowing an OB-GYN to serve as a primary care practitioner.
Bars plans from denying coverage of routine patient costs for patients with life-threatening or serious illness who join FDA- or NIH-approved clinical trials.

Requires a complaints and appeals process for coverage denials, including mandatory use of an outside review panel, and restricts incentive arrangements with providers that could reward limiting care.

Requires each plan to give enrollees a standardized, three-page prospectus disclosing doctor-to-enrollee ratios, denial and appeal rates, physician payment incentive structures, exclusions, and copayments, making plans comparable.

Prohibits plans from interfering with doctor-patient medical communications, voiding any contract gag clause, and bars discrimination based on health status, genetic makeup, disability, or expected need for services.

analysis.who_pays: Managed care organizations and health insurers would bear the cost of compliance: wider provider networks, coverage of out-of-network specialists and clinical trial costs, outside appeal panels, and annual disclosure. Employer-sponsored plans and employers would face compliance costs, and plans would typically pass increased coverage and administrative costs into premiums and cost-sharing for enrollees.

drawbacks.text: The mandates would raise plan costs: guaranteeing access to out-of-network specialists, paying routine clinical-trial costs, running outside review panels, and producing annual disclosure documents are all new expenses plans would generally recover through higher premiums, and critics of federal benefit mandates argued such requirements push employers toward dropping coverage altogether. The bill contained no provision to offset those costs.

The bill relied heavily on regulations to be written later by the Secretary of Health and Human Services, so the strength of many rights would have depended on the details of rulemaking rather than the statute itself.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For enrollees, the protections are broad and concrete: the emergency-care standard, outside appeals, clinical trial coverage, and standardized disclosure directly address the practices that most often leave patients stuck with denied care. The genuine cost is that these are mandates on plans and employers without any subsidy, so the burden lands in premiums and, at the margin, in some employers' willingness to offer coverage. The bill was also unusually sweeping for its time, applying to nearly every type of coverage at once, which would have made the compliance transition significant. On balance, the patient protections are real and the cost objection, while fair, was the standard argument against any patient-rights mandate.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in November 1997 with no cosponsors, sent to the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee, and the committee never took it up, so it died when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.

narrative.text: Sen. Barbara Boxer introduced the bill on November 9, 1997, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources.
The committee took no further action; the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote, and the Congress ended on January 3, 1999.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Managed care organizations, health insurers, and employer-sponsored plans are better off because the bill never advanced: none of its coverage mandates, appeal requirements, or disclosure rules took effect, and no compliance costs were imposed. Enrollees gained none of the promised rights, though other narrower patient-rights proposals circulated in the same period.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Managed care insurers and employer plans

for.name: Barbara Boxer
for.role: U.S. Senator (D-CA); sole sponsor of the bill
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Health Insurance Consumer's Bill of Rights Act in the Senate and delivered introductory remarks on it.

against.name: Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further action on it for the rest of the Congress; no hearing, markup, or vote was ever held.

against.name: Jim Jeffords
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee of referral, never scheduled action on the bill during the 105th Congress.

against.name: Managed care industry
against.role: Health insurers and HMO trade groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed comprehensive federal patient-rights mandates on managed care plans during the late-1990s patient bill of rights debate.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, so no roll-call record exists; the bill's only sponsor was a Democrat, it drew zero cosponsors of either party, and it sat in a committee run by Republicans.

industries.industry: Managed care plans and health insurers (HMOs)
industries.note: The bill would have required them to widen networks, cover out-of-network specialists and clinical trials, waive prior authorization for emergencies, run outside appeals, and disclose denial rates and physician payment incentives. Because this industry earns revenue by managing and limiting care, its interest in avoiding these mandates ran against the enrollees who would have benefited from them.

Employer plans would have been directly required to comply with the bill of rights under ERISA and the Internal Revenue Code amendments, adding compliance and coverage costs typically passed into premiums.

industries.industry: Physicians, especially specialists and OB-GYNs, and emergency care providers
industries.note: Standing referrals, direct OB-GYN access, non-network coverage, and bans on gag clauses would have expanded what plans must pay physicians to provide.

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefit managers and formulary-restricted drug coverage
industries.note: Plans with drug formularies would have had to disclose the restrictions and grant medically necessary exceptions, modestly constraining formulary management while leaving the formulary structure itself in place.
